messages.subject: negative observed variable variance
parts:
Hey all,
I tested the following model, which fits quite well. See summary outpur below.

model_10_5 <- '
# latent variables
forest_management =~ ForMI+SMI
biodiversity_herbs =~ shannon_herbs + Simpsons_herbs
forest_structure =~ mts+MTS_N
light =~ mean_LEC_corr+H_ell_weighted
soil =~ Sand#+Clay

# direct effects: regressions
forest_structure  ~ forest_management + soil
light ~ forest_structure
biodiversity_herbs ~ forest_management + soil + forest_structure

# (co)variances
Sand ~~ H_ell_weighted+mean_LEC_corr
ForMI ~~ H_ell_weighted+mean_LEC_corr
'



sem_10_5 <- sem(model_10_5, data=df_sem10_5_f, ordered = c("mts"))
summary(sem_10_5,fit.measures=T,rsquare=T)

However some observed variable variance is negative, wich causes problems when I want to go through a followup sensitivity analysis with my model.
I've read halfway through http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/0049124112442138 to get an idea of before realising, that I didn't understand what I was reading.
I'd be very happy if anyone could translate the journal, that surly contains the answer to my question into a language, that I'd understand.

messages.subject: Re: negative observed variable variance
parts: I resolved my problems by using mctest() function of package mctest. literally all of my indicator variables were multicollinear. I now used the same model without latent variables after choosing one indicator as most predicative.

messages.subject: Re: negative observed variable variance
parts:
I've read halfway through http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/0049124112442138 to get an idea of before realising, that I didn't understand what I was reading.
I'd be very happy if anyone could translate the journal, that surly contains the answer to my question into a language, that I'd understand.

The short story is that a Heywood case could be due to either sampling error or gross misspecification.  If your model does not fit terribly, it is unlikely to be the cause of the Heywood case.  But in small samples, Heywood cases are quite common for parameters that are near the boundary.  So before trying to solve the "problem" of a negative variance (or correlation > 1), test whether there is any evidence that it is a problem to begin with.  If your interval estimate (e.g., a 95% CI) for the negative variance includes positive values, then you can't reject the null hypothesis that the true variance is positive, and the negative point estimate is reasonably consistent with mere sampling error.  

summary(sem_10_5, fit = TRUE, rsq = TRUE, ci = TRUE)
